There is something peculiarly gratifying in the thought, that there is one who loves us þÿ who makes our interest his own. My hearers þÿ Love, as truly says my text hiay be linked to a thousand things þÿ things Consistent, things contrariant, things anomalous, things paradoxical, and things plausible; but I shall mention only a few, besides thfe vulture and dove, to which this tender (yet terrible tough) passioh may be linked. Love, then, is like the devil ; because it torments usi and hath a warm place for its home. It is like the consumption ; because it wastes away the flesh, alternately pales and reddens the Cheek, and sets doctors at defiance. It is like heaven; because it wraps the soul in & blanket of bliss, and makes a fellow feel as though forever ought to be lengthened ahd eternity widehed, to give it scope for the ex-t pansion of its jovs. It is like salt; because it gives a relish to the cold porridge of poverty. It is like pepper; because it is warming to the inwards, ahd sometimes brings tears to the eyes It is like sugar ; because it is sweet, and dealt out by spoonful at the teatable. It is like wine ; because it makes us happy, and talk nonsense enough to physic a Cast iron phoenix. It is like a ship; because it rides upon both calm and troubled seas, and takes one to the wished for port. It is like a jack o'lantern ; because it leads one into a bog, and the more a body struggles to get out, the deepei he is in the mire. It is like the bite of a mad dog, or the kiss of a pretty Woman ; because they both make a man run

mad. My friends love, among other things, is þÿ like a rose tree; because it hath both thorns and blossoms. The blossoms are fragrant and beautiful, but the thorns are sharp and piercing. It blooms for a short season, and then is lovely no more. Soon the green leaves of friendship turn yellow and fall ; and thCre stands the unsightly tree of loVe, as barren of beauty as a flying fish is ol feathers ! It is like the small pox ; because those who have once been afflicted with it are not liable to have it again, except in a milder form. It is like the measles ; because it is severer with adults, than with children. It is like the rain : because it falls " upon the just and unjust." Like death; because it is no respecter of persons. Like a shadow ; because it sticks close to its object. Like a tick upon a sheep ; because it cannot be shaken off. þÿ When Napoleon took possession of Hoi Like a wife; because there is no getting rid of it. Like a goose ; because it is silly. Like a rabbit s because there is nothing like it, Like a monkey ; because it makes mischief. In short, love is like a ghost ; because it is like everything and like nothing þÿ often talked about but never seen, touched or understood.

They have passed away as vapor, while nature wore the same aspect of beauty as when her Creator comm anded her to be. The heavens shall be as bright over our gruves as they are now around our paths. The world will tiave the same atli action lor our offspring yet unborn, as she bad once for ourselves, and tfiat she lias now for our children. Yet a little while and all this will have happened The throbbing heart will be slihed, and we shall be at rest. Our funeral will wind on its way, and the prayers will be said, and our friends return, and we shall be left behind to darkness and the worm. And it may be for some short time that we shall be spoken of, but the tilings of lite will creep in and we shall soon be forgotten. Shortly after leaving the city we met several flocks of sheep, preceded bv their shopherds, walking slowly towards Jerusalem, and at once the lull force of all the beautiful imagery, and the many touching similes derived from such scenes and such associations, and so often alluded to in Scripture came vivHIy before me. "these Arab shepherds, tlad in the simple Abbas of their class and carrvitlg a Wooden crook walked in front. The sheep, which are a peculiar and bandsome breed are mostly low sized ; the foreparts of their bodies are of a fawn colour, the hinder parts while, they have long pendant silken ears and sweeping tails, their faces more oval and longer than the species in these countries, and they have altogether a more pleasing, docile, and mild expression of countenance. Not one of them ever ventured before the shepherd, hut stopped or quickened their pace as he did ; or if the young and froward creature lagged behind or stiayed to either side, a single word from their leader, often a verv look brought it back and checked its wanderings; A lew favourite lambs frisked about their master, rubbing themselves against his legs and garments. After the sheep came some young goats and lambs, and the Whole procession closed \Vith about two dozen of old patriarchial looking goats, Which brought up the rear. These goats have long horns and pendant cirs that hang almost to the ground, and their hair is a glossy black and of the finest grain ; the sheep aod goats were perfectly

distinct- ' These shepherds are often to be seen about sunset slowlv approaching the city from all sides, to seek shelter for their flocks, during the night, in some of the deep valleys by 'Vhich it is surrounded carrying the lambs in their bosoms. It is almost incredible the influence that the shepherds of Palestine possess over their flocks ; many ol them have no dogs, but a word is quite sufficient to make them understand and obey the will of their shepherd. He sleeps among them at night, and in the morning leads them forth to pasture altvitys walking before them, guiding them to lh«»se places where they can enjov the best of food, and resting when he thinks they have obtained a sufficiency, or during the heat of the day, in some cool shady place where they all immediately lie down around hint. He has generally two or three favorite lambs which do not mix with the flock, but follow close at his side frisking and fondling about liiin like dogs ; indeed the degree of intelligence and understanding that exists between the Arab and Ins flock is really astonishing. " They know his voice and follow him and he careth for the sheep." It was probably to such shepherds as these that the angel announced the glad tidings of the Saviour's þÿbirth, Wild's Narratives.

The Convent of tlte Capuchin. 'The celebrated Convent of the Capuchins, about a mile without the city of Palermo, contains nothing very remarkable but its burial place, which is indeed a singular curiosity. This is a vast subterranean apartment divided into galleries, the walls on each side of which are hollowed into a variety of niches, as if intended for a great collection of statues. In-

3 "Jf. A'rr3» I . .1 stead of statues, these niches are filled with dead bodies, set upright on their legs and secured by the back to the inside of the niche. The number of these is not less tlmn three thousand ; and all being dressed in the clothes they usually wore, they form a most respec table and venerable assembly. The skin and muscles, by a certain preparation, become as dry and hard as a piece of stock fish, and although many of them have been here upwards of twohundredand fifty years, yet none are reduced to skeletons: the muscles indeed, in some, appear to be a good deal more shrunk than in others j probably because these persons had been more attenuated at the time of their death. Here the people of Palermo pay daily visits to their deceased friends, and recall with pleasure and regret the scenes of theit past life ; here they familiarize themselves witlt their future state, and choose the company they would wish to keep in the other world. It is a common tiling to make choice of their niche: the bodies of the princes and first nobility are lodged in handsome chests or trunks, some of them richly adorned t these are not in the shape of coffins, hut all of one width, and about a foot and a half or two leet deep. 'The keys are kept by the nearest relations of the family, who sometimes come and drop a tear over their depailed friends. From Hotce Sicilianee. by Signor Satrotore Abbate E. ber of the Oregon þÿlegislature. þÿ The fisheries of the country nre very great, and foremost among all the varieties which they produce is the unrivalled salmon. It would be impossible to estimate the numbers of this excellent fish annually taken in the Columbia and its tributaries 5 but they have been set down at 10 000 barrels a year, þÿ which number 1 do not by any means think too large. All the salmon caught here are taken by the Indians and sold to the whites at about 10 cents each, and frequently for less. One Indian will lake about 20 on an average per day. There are several other kinds of fish in tiie bays( riveis. and creeks of the territory, of which a species of Cod and the sturgeon are the most important. The latter are large fish, and afford great sport in a leisure hour to take them with a hook and line. Of shell fish we have the crab, clams, muscles, and a small description of oysters þÿ In regard to the products of the field, the agricultural parts of Oregon, or those of the first section, "yield wheat, it is said, from 20 to 40 bushels to the acre, and that of superior quality. Indian corn and sweet potatoe do not thrive. Oafs, peas, tomatoes, garden vegetables, Irish potatos and turnips, have succeeded to advantage. Apples, peaches, cherries, plums, pears, and melons may be yielded. An abundant growth of grass favours raising of cattle, the wappatoo, a peculiar root growing there, being profitably used for fattening hogs.

The Collision off Beaciiy-H had. þÿ The Unexpected return of the Seringa patam East Indiaman to Blackwall on Wednesday alterttoon, in an apparently disabled slate, attracted considerable attention, and a large crowd of persons assembled on the pier to witness her arrival, as on the previous day it had been reported that she bad been in collision With a large Danish West Indiaman, which was totally lost in the Channel. The Sefingapatam, which is the property of Mr. Green, the eminent shipbuilder and owner of Bluckwall, is one of the large class Indiamcn, being 1,000 þÿtons burden. She left the East India Docks on Saturday afternoon, and Gravesend on the following day, ar.d proceeded out to sea on her way to Portsmouth, to take on board the passengers for the ports she was bound for þÿ Madras and Calcutta. þÿ On Monday evening she was nearing Bea chyhead, steering the usual course down the Channel, and going favourably before the wind, which was blowing N. and N. E.-- Later in the night the breeze is stated to have freshened up and at about 1 1 þÿo clock she was travelling through the water at the rate of nine knots an hour. Before this period, it should be observed, a vessel was seen heating up, and to all appearance was heavilyladen. Whether a proper look out was kept on board the Seriugapatam is a circumstance that we have been unable to elicit. We aro told that the captain was to join the Indiaman at Portsmouth and that a Downs pilot had charge of her sailing. Eor a short time no

danger appeared to exist, hut suddenly the ship, which afterwards turned out to he the Harriet, laden with sugar from St. Croix to Copenhagen, was noticed to steer a course close under the Seringnpalam's bows. They hailed each other, but the crew of the Harriet, probably being foreigners, and unacquainted with the English language, were confused, as also tlmse on hoaid the Indiaman. The result was, tlut in the course of a few minutes both vessels came in collision. The Seringapatam struck the Harriet amidships, and being almost treble her size, the concussion on 'he latter was tremendous, cutting her down to the water's edge, and carrying away her mainmast. Such was the force, in fact, that the Harriet was thrown almost on her beam ends, and her instant foundering seemed inevitable. Those of her crew who formed the watch instantly ran up the fore and mizen masts, and jumped on to the bowsprit of the Seringapatnm, and shortly afierwards the remainder of the crew, who were below in bed, followed in a state of nudity. They had scarcely done so when her remaining ninsts broke sharp off. and went overboard. By some means her rigging got entangled with the bow of the Indiaman. but as the Harriet filled, the pressure carried away all forward þÿ viz-, the bowsprit, jibboom, and other spars of the Seringapotam, clean olf by the hull, and the ship rolling over for a ti nr, disappeared. Luckily, the Seringapatarn sustained no other damage, although so terrible was the collision that her crew feared
she would founder, but the continued sounding of the pumps showed that she was not even making þÿwater.- (Hohe.

s c t> a x i'n was apprised by the þÿLloyd s agent at East, , mandmg armies in the field, he could beurne of the discovery by some pilots of a large vessel in the Channel, o(l Beachy head which appeared to have been abandoned by her crew, and at the same lime requested to send a steam packet out to tow the vessel into harbour. The Magnet was, accordingly, despatched shortly after midnight, and succeeded in falling in with the vessel. It was found keel uppermost, and proved to lie the Danish bark Harriet, from St. Croix to Copenhagen, laden with sugar and rum. On Wednesday the 22d the Lord Mayor gave an entertainment to her Majesty's ministers and a large party in the Egypiian Hall. 1 Lore were about 260 ladies and gentlemen present. A magnificent array of plate glittered on every side of the hall, and it being a lull dress party, the gay attire and hand some uniforms contributed to make the whole spectacle very imposing and august. þÿ We give one of .Sir K. þÿPeel s speeches at the festive þÿscene. Peel then rose and said, þÿ 1 am permitted by the Lord Mayor to give a toast which is not upon the list of toasts which lias been prepared ; 1 am certainly departing from the established usage which prevails <>n these festive occasions, but nevei the less 1 feel the utmost confidence that it is a toast which will he received by you witii thegieaiesl satisfaction, and even enthusiasm 1 beg to propose The Health of the King of the þÿ þÿFrench (loud and prolonged cheering.) I believe that, under any circumstances, the toast would he acceptable your feelings to on account of the high personal character of the King, and on account of the friendly relations which have long subsisted between tins country and France, the maintenance of which, uninterrupted, is of such importance to the welfare and to the peace of Europe. It would he peculiarly acceptable to the City of Eondon, think, I on account of the manner in which the King of the French received iis representatives, and expressed his cordial

satisfaction in having from them a maik of their esteem and respect (hear). But, gentlemen, events have recently occurred which will make you more than ordinarily anxious to join in this toast (hear, hear). It is, I think, important that we should show that that cry of indignation which has been raised through Fiance, at these base and cowardly and iiila mous attempts at assassination (hear) is re echoed on the hanks of the Thames (cheers). It has pleased Almighty God to frustrate these repeated ellorts to assassinate that great Sovereign (hear, hear). Bui good, permanent good, has resulted from the attempt so frustrated. Ii fins given the King the opportunity of manifesting a decree of personal courage nnd fortitude and heroism, which, as he has not the opportunity of com

hardly have displayed, excepting under the extraordinary circumstances in which he lias been placed (cheers) : and to a gallant people like the people of "France, eminent for their own bravery, and admiring bravery in others, I can conceive noihing which is more calculated to recommend their King to iheir affection and attachment than those signal instances of personal courage winch have been displayed by fiinr under the circumstances in which he has, as I have said, been placed (renewed cheers) Gentlemen, 1 am sure it will he agreeable to Englishmen to mark their indignation of these detestable crimes (loud cries of hear, þÿhear ), and to otter our sympathy to that illustrious lady the Queen of the french (great cheering), who has shared adversity with him, who has shared his prosperity, who has shared his dangers (hear, hear), and who by her high character and exemplary virtues hastluown a lushe upon the exalted station which she has reached (cheers). It will be agieeable to you to mark your sympathy with that noble family (hear, hear), not merely noble by iis birth, but which has that other patent of nobility, that all the sons are brave, and all the daughter are virtuous (enthusiastic cheering). Gentlemen, I am confident you will, by diinling this toast with enthusiasm, express your concurrence in my earnest prayer that it may long please Almighty God to protect the life of that Sovereign, for the benefit of his own country, and for the advantage of the world ; that by the continuance of that-dife

Loss of a Swedish Sloop of War þÿ Seventeen Pe rsons only saved out of a crew of one Hundred and thirty two. þÿ hast evening, between the hours of eleven and twelve o'clock, the barque Swan, Capt. Snell, from New Orleans, arrived at this port, and is now lying at the fiist wharf above Pine street She brings the following lamentable news t On the 3d of May, (Sunday.) about four þÿo clock in the afternoon, in latitude 2 5 deg. 11 minutes, and longitude 19 degrees, 42 minutes, between Havana and the Floridas the captain observed something at a distance, which he took for a piratical vessel, and immediately ordered the guns of the barque to be loaded and in a few minutes every thing about the vessel was in prime order and ready lor action. He was, however, upon arriving near the supposed pirates, corrected in his views, and discovered that they were persons who had been wrecked þÿ and were blistered by the sun in a horrible manner, and in a state of nudity floating upon spars and pieces of þÿ wood. There were seventeen in number, all of whom were taken on board and every possible care taken of them by the captain and crew of the barque. Their story is as follows. þÿ On the fust of May the Swedish sloop of war Charles Krona, Captain (E. G. Klint), sailed from Havana for Sweden, with a crew consisting of one hundred and thirty two men, and when off' MatanZas, having been two days and three nights out, was caught in a

Squall, which turned the vessel bottom upward, consigning to a watery grave one hundred and fifteen souls l The vessel immediately sunk. The seventeen above alluded to saved themselves by clinging to the spars of the vessel and pieces of wood, upon which they floated and buffeted the angry waves for one day and night, when they were picked up, almost in a stale of starvation, and brought to this city bv the barque Swan, and the only officer saved was first Lieutenant A. F. Thersmeden, who is stopping at þÿBloodgood s foot of Walnut street þÿ Lieutenants Suerin, Bilt, and Bevcnstrole, were the names of the officers who were lost. Maonetic Teleuk Arn. The use of this wonderful invention was admirably illnstiaed one day this week, in the course of a trial in the District Court. The turning point of the case, by a train of unexpected testimony, became almost entirely changed, and depended upon an entry in a book which was in New York. It was near the hour of adjournment, and the counsel sent a despatc h by telegraph to New York to aseeitain the exact nature of the entry. He became satisfied with the answer, sent another despatch with orders to firing on tiie book, and a witness to verify it, immediately. All this was done while the trial was going on and without the counsel leaving the court room. The Court adjourned without concluding the case; by 10 þÿo clock that night the witness and the book wete in the city, botli were thoroughly examined by the counsel, and the next morning were produced in Court. Had the ordinary methods of mail communication been depended upon, word could not have been transmitted to New York and answer returned until at least thirty six huuis alter the case had been concluded. Another instance of the rapidity of communication by the lightning line occnried about the same time to another member of the bar. His clients reside in Boston, and from the manner in which cases were disposed of, it became very probable that (heir's would be reached. The attorney sent a telegraphic despatch to New York in lime for that day's Boston mail, and tiie insult was that the parties nod witnesses wete warned in season,

and were in this city ready for 1 1 ini at t lie proper Itour. From the St. Thomas Times, þÿ 23rd May 1846. FRENCH TRA NS- A TL .1 A TIC STEAMERS. We notice in t he Courrier du Havre that the French government has contracted with a Company to run a line ot powerful steamers between Havre, New York, Havana, and the French colonies in the West Indies. The particulars of the routes ate not yet announced, hut we trust that th s port will be one of the points of visit. Compel it ton will benefit the travelling public, lor the tares by the lloval VV l Mail Company are still too high, and out of the reach of persons of limited means, who have a light to expect accommodation as well as those possessed of weighty purses. The French boats can be run at less expense we imagine as far as the table is concerned, but the coaling, salaries, and other contingencies must be much the same. It is to be hoped that they will not encounter so many disasters as the English line did in the early part of its career, for if it be fortunate it will be able we should think to carry passengers and freight for fully one third less than the present rales. The affairs of the English company are now improving and they too could afford a reduction, nor would they be losers, for the increase of the transit would compensate for it.

ROYAL MAIL STEAM-PACKET COM PAS Y. The annual meeting of this company was held on the 9th of April, at the London Tavern, liishopsgate street; Andrew Cohille Esq was called to the chair, the president of the company having died lately. There was a more than usually large attendance of proprietors upon the occasion. The secretary read the report of the directors for the past year, in which they congratulated the proprietors upon the tael, that, for the past year, their expectations, notwithstanding it was a year of great depression, had not only been realised but considerably surpassed ; that the accounts of the company for the past year exhibited as compated wiih the year 1814, a considerable augmentation. The receipts for freight and passage money, outward, homeward, and international, showed an increase ; which, in the aggregate amounted, upon freight, to over £5.358, and upon passage money to over £16,446, making a total upon those two items of over £21.804. The charges for insurance in 1845 amounted to £1,828, which arose out of transactions that took place in the year 1844, leaving to the credit of that account £23,171, which had been invested in the Three and a quart per Cent stock. The shifts had been maintained in the highest state of efficiency. The directors had been able to replace the capital that had previously written off, to the amount of £79,790 ; but the shareholders must recollect that in the estimates of assets the value of the ships had been returned at their origi-

nal cost, without any deduction for four þÿveat s wear, and, therefore, it would be necessary hereafter to create a reserved fund to cover that deterioration. The company had purchased the Eagle, and bad contracted lor another new vessel. The Admiralty had entered into contracts, with the pacific Steam Navigation Company to convey passengers monthly to and fro between Panama, Callao, Valparaiso and the intermediate ports, in connexion with this þÿcompany s hips running

between Jamaica and Chagrcs. The directo i s had deemed it important to encoutage the conveyance of treasure across the Isthmus t>f Panama and therefore, the company had undertaken to transport it over land by agents appointed for that purpose. The report concluded by declaring a dividend of 30s per share, or at the rate of five per cent, per annum on the paid up capital, for the half year up to last December. The state' merit of the accounts of the þÿcompany s receipts and disbursements lor the past year was then handed about, by which it appeared that the total disbursements amounted to £'271,588, 5s- 5d., which left a surplus of £111 15s. lid, Mr. Stewart congratulated the meeting upon the prosperous slate of their affairs, and said he considered that the thanks of the company were due to the directors for the admirable manner in which they had conducted their affairs, particularly when he reminded the meeting that now they had a very large sum to their credit, while in the year 1842 they were considerably in debt on the shipping account. þÿ He had great pleasure in proposing a vote ol thanks to them þÿ (Cheers. ) The report was then unanimously adopted the vote of thanks to the chairman and directors passed by acclamation. Captain Shepperd elected as chairman (in the room of Mr. Irvint;, deceased,) the auditors re elected, and the meeting separated.

Orange Syrup. þÿ This syrup is so easily made, and can be used so constantly to advantage, that no housekeeper should be without it. Select ripe and thin-skinned fruit, squeeze the juice through a sieve ; to every point add one and a half pound of powdered sugar, boil it slowly, and skim as long as any scum rises: you may then lake it off, let it grow cold, and bottle it off. Be sure to secure the corks well. Two tablespoonfuls of this syrup, mixed in melted butter, make an admirable sauce for plum or batter pudding ; it imparts a fine flavour, and a teaspoonful introduced into a glass of punch adds much to its deliciousness.

IS THE OK EGOS QUESTIOS SETTLED ? Humours begin to he circulated in the newspapers, on both sides ol the Atlantic, tha t the Oregon question is settled þÿ or about to be si þÿllied or, at least, that propostons are about to he made by the British government, which will lead to a very early settlement of all differences between the two nations- The Journal of Commerce, of this city, a paper that has always a large stock of religion and hypocrisy on hand, states that letters from the highest source were received by the þÿ Great þÿWestern, giving the details of this þÿsettlement namely on the parallel of forty nifie, to the straits ol Fuca ; and along those Straits to the þÿPacific giving the whole of Vancouvers Island to Great Britain, with the navigation of the Columbia river, for a limited term of years, ll is also added that these terms will be accepted by Mr Polk shaped into a treaty and confirmed by the Senate. We have also rumours from Washington, that Mr. Polk has given the notice quit, to to the British Minister, who will forthwith re-open the negocialious on the terms indicated. These rumouis on re opening the negociation þÿ and also staling the teims we give tor what tliev are worth ; hut we doubt tlu-ir accuracy iu a number of important particulars. The Journal of Commerce, thinks that the terms proposed will be acceded to by Mr Polk, and confirmed by the Senate : but it is very well known that these editors are very easily deceived, iu consequence of the ex-

treme i merest which they feel in lavor ol a certain exaggerated view they take of the question Any treaty giving the whole of þÿVancouver s island, unconditionally, to the iiriiish government, we do not believe will receive the sanction of two thirds ot the United Slates Senate. Vancouver's Island is the key þÿ the Gibralþÿter of the navigation of the Oregon territory. It commands the outlets and inlets to all the harbours of any value in that country including þÿPuget s Sound, Admiralty Inlet, tSoc. A fortification on the south end of that island, would command all these harbours, and give England complete naval control over the entire territory, and the coast that surrounds it, as much as Gibralter gives Her over the Mediterranean. We are persuaded this sort of treaty will never be confirmed by the Senate. Indeed, we know the opinions of many of those democratic Senators who arc in favor of the forty ninth parallel, who will yet vote against a treaty which would recognise the right of England to t lie whole of þÿVancouver sIsland, with the liberty of fortifying it as they choose, ll lias been suggested, indeed, that England may agree never to eteet a fortification on the island, if she should receive it under the terms ol a treaty : but such a security would he rather equivocal.

According fto a!) these rumours, probabilities, and facts, it may be reasonable to believe that negotiations will be opened at Washington, on some amicable basis, under the action taken by the President on the notice question ; but we have yet many doubts of an early settlement of the question between Mr. Polk and Mr. Pakenham. Both these statesmen þÿ the President and the Plenipotentiary, are honorable, amiable and worthy men great þÿ men in little matters ; but their previous Treatment of these mighty negotiations, and the blunderings which they have already exhibited, show that they are hardly equal to the emergency which destiny in one ©I its freaks, has placed them in, ns negotiators upon an important question between two great and leading nations of the world þÿ in which the mighty questions of peace or war mainly depend. Let us hope for the best but prepare for the worst. A7. ¥. Ihrahl. þÿ þÿ þÿ»000« From the London Morning Herald.

(PROM OUR OWN CORRESPONDENT ) Lisbon, April 20. Serious disturbances have taken place in Some parts of the province of Minho. As yet, all we know on the subject is what has been communicated by telegraph, viz, þÿ That on the 1 4 1 h instant the people ol the districts of Guimaroes, Prado, and Penella, rose tumultuously, and entering the city of Braga aitacked the 8th Infantry there stationed, by whom they were driven back Willi the loss of m.mv killed and þÿwounded.' ture with a Wolf. þÿ The post expected to day from t he north will no doubt biing foil particulars of the affair ; anil, if in time lor the mail, I shall not fail to add them in a postscript. Troops have already been sent from this city, whence it may be inferred that seme danger appre- is hended. The government and iis friends labour to make it appear that the revolt has been bi ought about bv the machinations of agents sent from this city or Oporto by the Septembrist party ; but t here is no doubt that it is really t he spontaneous outbreak of an over taxed anti oppressed population who feel that they have received no benefit of any sort as a set off against the crushing burdens imposed upon them þÿ not alone in taxes to the state, but what is far more vexatious in lees and emoluments without end for the support, in ease and luxury of the swarm of hungry employes who aie battening upon the fat, aye and the lean too, of the land and for whose behoof the utmost ingenuity has been shown in devising modes of

extorting money from the pockets of the people, The salaries of the public functionaries are but small, and yet, see how they live! Look at those in the highest grade, and see them with their salaries of about 600/ a year, living like men ol large fortune, sporting splendid equipages with well powdered flunkies in red plush, giving entertainments nil the most magnificent scale, and still affording out of their savings to buy castles, palaces and estates. Then tracing down to the other end of the chain, just observe the wife of that ninth rate understrapper, flaunting about the public promenades with as much I'Ve itch milliner)' and bijouterie atmiil her as must have cost at least n half vear's salary Ian all this be done fairly? Of course not Salary goes but a little way, and the rest is made up of douceurs, fees, fines, and emoluments, Wtuug from the peo-

2'X. C 3s 0 3 X. A 7 3 3» ple in a thousand different ways. Exempli gratia : the new sanatory law, like the former one, requires that before a corpse can be filtered, a certificate ol the cause ol death should be obtained from the authority whose office it is to ascertain it. But formerly the etiarge for the certificate was a mere trifle, and now it is whatever the authority in question may please to make it. In some parts of the country it has been fixed at two mil. reis, or uoout ten shillings, a most enormous tax upon the poor ; and hence have already arisen some disturbances in different places but citielly in the province where the more serious outbreak lias now occurred. This system is so oppressive that no government persisting in it Cjin hope to escape a heavy retribution ; ami it may safely be predicted that unless the evil be averted in time by a complete sweeping away of all the pe,ty extortions to which the people of this country are subjected lor the sole use and benefit of the employes, there will soon be an end to the public tiunquillity which it is the boast of the piesont government to have secured. The Minho disturbances will no doubt soon be put down by sabre and bayonet j but as the grievances which prompted them are not local nut general, the triumph of the govern ment will only render it more hateful to the people, and lead to other and pet haps mote formidable outbursts of popular indignation.

t ga&ji mo if s Extraordinary and Dangerous Adven- Last week a woman livmg in the parish of Redtnatley, in the county ol Worcester, ongoing into an outhouse, adjoining her cottage, observed what she supposed to be a large dog, lying in one corner of the building; and thinking it to belong to some drover, took no further notice ol it. Destination of the Mormons þÿ It is thought by many that the Mormon war may be considered as at an end. The Mormons have pledged themselves, verbally and in writing, to leave the state of Illinois next spring. General Harden, in his letter communicating the arrungement, say s it is the intention of the Mormons to locale themselves west of the Rocky Mountains The St Louis Republican says þÿ: Nootka or Vancouver Island, on the north west coast of North America, is to be the final destination and borne of the Mormon people. This island is about 300 miles long, and from 75 to 100 in width It is separated from the main land tty a long narrow strait, and lies between the 47th or 48th and 51st or 52d degrees of north latitude, extending along the coast in a north- 'vest direction. The boundary line between the American and the British possessions in the uoith west will probably pass across the island. The English, we believe, have one or two trading posts on the island ; but for the most part it is inhabited by Indians of a not warlike disposition. It is a long journey, but can be accomplished. If the Mormons do emigrate to that distant land, they will be nut of the reach of harm from white rnen, and may enjoy their peculiar notions in quiet, until tire Devil breeds his own discords and confusion among þÿthem. The Republican understands, from the same authority, that companies are rapidly organising at Nauvoo, for an early start in the spring. The Church authorities and leading men will go out in a
very large company, and, without doubt, the remainder will follow.

Ceremony of Opening Parliament. þÿ The precise formalizes observed at the opening of Parliament, by the Sovereign person, will in be read with interest. Her Majesty, having proceeded in state to the House of Lords, where " seated on the throne, adorned with her crown and regal ornaments, and attended by her officers of state." (all the Lords being in tiieir robes, and standing while her Majesty is present), she commands the Gentleman Usher of the black Rod, through the Great Lord Chamberlain, to let the Commons know, it is her Majesty's pleasure they attend her immediately in this house." The Usher of the Black Itod goes at once to the door of the House of Commons, which he strikes with his rod ; and on being admitted, he advances up the middle of the house toward the table, making three obeisances to the chair; and says, "Mr. Speaker, the Queen Commands this Honorable House to attend her Majesty immediately in the House of Peers " He then withdraws, still making obeisance, nor does be turn lus back upon the House until lie lias reached the bar. þÿ The Speaker, with the House, immediately goes up to the bar of the House of Lords, upon which the Queen reads her speech to both Houses of Parliament, which is delivered into her hands by the Lord Chancellor, kneeling on one knee. When her Majesty is not personally present, the causes of summons are declared by the Lords Commissioners. The Gentleman Usher of the Black Bod is sent, in the same manner, to the Common, and acqua tits the

Speaker that the Lords Commissioners desire the attendance of the Honorable House in the House of Peers, to hear the commission read; and when Mr. Speaker and the House have readied ihc bar ol the Peers, the Lord Chancellor reads the royal speech to both houses. When the speech lias been ddivered by her Majesty in person, or by commission, the House of Lords is adjourned during pleasure, and the Commons separate for an hour or two, without any formal adjournment ; and if any members desire to be swoin in on that day, it is usual fur the House to re assemble before 4 o'clock. Wtien the Houses are resumed in the afternoon, the main business is for the Lord Chancellor in the Lords and the Speaker in the Commons to report her Majesty's speech. In the former house the speech is read at length by the clerk, and in the hitter by the Speaker, who states that for greater arcuraey lie has obtained a copy. But before this is done it is the practice in boih houses lo read some bill a first time pro forma, in order to assert their right of deliberating without reference to the immediate cause of summons. This practice in the Lords is enjoined by a standing order. In the Commons, the same form is observed by ancient custom only. There is an entry on the journal of the 22nd March, 1003, þÿ " That the first day of every sitting in every Parliament, some one bill, and no more, received) a first reading for form's sake." This practice lias continued until the present time. By the Lord's standing order it
would appear necessary that this form should be observed immediately after the oaths have

Tii. r - i - x t ' been taken ; but in the Commons the bill is only required to be read before the report of the Queen's speech ; and other business is 0. instantly entered upon before the reading of the bill, as the issue of new writs, the consideration of matters of privilege, the presentation of papers, and the usual sessional orders and resolutions. When the royal speech has been read an address in answer to it is moved in both houses. Two members in each house are selee.ted by the Administration tor moving and seconding the address ; and they appear in their places in court dresses for that purpose. The address is an answer, paragraph by paragraph, to the Queen's speech. Amendments may bo made to any part of it, and when the question for an address, whether amended or not, has been agreed to, a select committee is appointed ' to prepare," or " draw up,'' an address. W lien the report is brought up by this committee amendments may still he made to die address before it is agreed to ; and after it has been finally agreed to, it is ordered to be presented to her Majesty. Wli.ii the speech has been delivered by the Queen in person, the address is presented by the whole House ; but when it has been lead by Lords Commissioners, t tie address oT the Upper House is delivered "by the Lords with white slaves" (i. e. bv Lords who hold appointments in the royal household.) and the address of the Commons by " such members of the House as are of her Majesty's Piivy Council." When the ad-

dress is to he presented by the whole House, " the Lords with while slave," in the one house, and the privy cmmcillois in the other are ordered to know her Majesty s plcasute when she will he attended wiili the address. Cn cli House meets, when it is understood that this ceremony will take place, and after her M aiesty's pleasure has been repoiled, proceeds separately to the Palace.

Surgical Operation on a Mesmeric Patient. þÿ The A etc York Herald coniuins a detailed account of the removal of a largo tumour from the hack of a young woman of colour in that city. The writer, who was sceptical us to the possibility ol the operation being peifoimed without the patient knowing it, alter describing the means " used to produce the mesmeric sleep, says: þÿ Dr, Kostwick first made a longitudinal incision, eight inches in length, through the flesh over the tumour, and then commenced cutting round it. When tfie knife was fust put in we wore watching the lace of the gill closely, expecting to see Iter start, and hear her scream : but there was not the slightest motion. She lay as still and motionless as a marble staiue. Not a quivering of the lip or of the eye lid could we observe. Llr. Hostwick, assisted by Dr. Chillis and Dr. Stearns, continued cutting away upon the tumour, and in thiee minutes it was taken out, there being, during the whole time, no motion on the (art of the girl. During the whole operation Dr. l'ike sat near the patient with Ins hand upon her head. Several physicians examined the pulse, and said it was apparently in a nntutnl state. Dr. Hostwick then, with a large darn ing needle, sewed up the incision, there still being no motion of muscle or nerve on the part of the patient. Alter placing adhesive plaster upon the incision, and bandaging it, Dr. Oltz (who, with Dr. Pike, had magnetised the patient) was called in to wake up the girl. This he did bv making passes over her

face : and upon waking she was told that the operation had not been performed, and that she must now have it done. This was done to see whether she would know anything about it. ' Well,' she said, she was sorry, but she w anted it taken out.' ' Do you feci no pain V asked Dr. Hostwick. 1 None,' said the girl. 'Have you felt none?' 'None.' was the answer again. She was then shown the tumour, and seemed to be very glad to see it out. It was an adipous tumour, and weighed li) ounces. We then left the house extremely puzzled. The time from which the operation was first commenced til! site was awakened was just 30 minutes."

MESSAGE THE Fit ESt DENT OF THE UNITED S l'A I LS, Communicating Information of the existing relations between the United Stales and Mexico, and recommending the adoption of measures for repelling the invasion committed by the Metiian forces upon the territory of the United Stales, May II, 1840.

1 lo the Senate and House of Representatives I The existing state of the relations between the United States and Mexico renders it proper that 1 should bring the subject to the consideration of Congress. In my message at the commencement of your present session the state of these relations, the causes which led to the suspension of diplomatic intercourse between the two countries in March, 1845. hnd the long-continued and unredressed Wrongs and injuries committed by the Mexican government on citizens of the United States, in their persons and property, were briefly set forth, As the facts and opinions which were then '.aid belore you were carefully considered, 1 cannot better express my present convictions of the condition ot affairs up to that time, than by referring you to that communication. The strong desire to establish peace with Mexico on liberal and honorable terms, and the readiness of this government to regulate and adjust our boundary, and other causes of difference with that power, on such fair and equitable principles as would lead to permanent relations of tiic most friendly nature, induced tne in September last to seek the fcopening of diplomatic relations between the two countries. Every measure adopted ori our part had for its object the furtherance of these desired results. In communicating to Congress a succinct statement of the injuries which we had suffered from Mexico, and whirfi have been accumulating during a period of more than twenty yeais, every ex-

pulsion that could tend lo inflame the people of Mexico, or defeat or delay a pacific result, was carefully avoided. An envoy of the United States repaired to Mexico, with full power to adjust every existing difference. But though present on the Mexican soil, by agreement between the two governments, invested with full powers, and bearing evidence of the most friendly dispositions, his mission has been unavailing. The Mexican government not only refused to receive him, or listen to his propositions, but, after a long continued series of menaces, have at last invaded our territory, and shed the blood of our fellow citizens on onr own soil. It now becomes my duty to state more in detail the origin, progress, and failure of that mission. In pursuance of the instructions given in September last, an inquiry was made, on the thirteenth of October, 1845. in the mosi friendly terms, through our consul in Mexico, of the minister for foreign affairs, whether the Mexican government " would receive an envoy from the Uniied Slates entrusted with full powers to adjust nil the questions in dispuie between the two governments;'' with the assurance that " should the answer be in the alfiruiative, such an envoy would be immediately despatched to Mexico." The Mexican minister, on the fifteenth of October, gave an affirmative answer to ibis

inquiry, requesting, at the same time, that our naval force at Vera Cruz might be withdrawn, lest its continued presence might assume the appearance of menace and coercion pending the negotiations. This force was immediately withdrawn. On the 10th of November, 1845, Mr. John Slidell, of Louisiana, was commissioned by me as envoy extraordinary and minister plenipotentiary of the United States to Mexico, and was en trusted with full powers to adjust both the questions of the Texas boundary and of indemnification to our citizens. The redress of the wrongs of our citizens naturally and inseparably blended itself with the question of boundary. The settlement of the one question, in any correct view of the subject, involves that of the other. 1 could not, for a moment, entertain the idea that the claims of our much injured and long suffering citizens, many of which had existed for more than twenty years, should be postponed, or separated from the settlement of the boundary question. Mr. Slidell arrived at Vera Cruz on the 30th of November, and was courteously received by the authorities of that city, lint the government of General Herrera was then tottering to its fall. The revolutionary party had seized upon the Texas question to effect or hasten its overthrow, lis determination to restore friendly relations with the United States, and to receive our minister, to negotiate for the settlement of this question, was violently assailed, and was made the great theme of denunciation against it. The gov.

eminent of General Herrera, there is good reason to believe, was si nceiely desiious to receive our minister ; but it yielded to the storm raised by its enemies, and on the 21st of December refused to accredit Mr. Slidell upon the most frivolous pretexts. These are so fully and ably exposed in the note of Mr Slidell, of the 24th of December last, to the Mexican minister of foreign relations, herewith transmitted, that I deem it unnecessary to enter into further detail on this portion of the subject. Five days after the date of Mr. Slidell's note, General llerrera yielded the government to General Fa redes, without a struggle, and on the 30th of December resigned the presidency. This revolution was accomplished solely by the army, the people having taken little part in the contest ; and thus the supreme power in Mexico passed into the hands of a military leader. Determined to leave no effort untried to effect an amicable adjustment with Mexico, 1 directed Mr. Slidell to present his credentials lo the government of General I'aredes, and ask to be officially received by him. There would Itave been less ground for taking this step had General Paredos come into power by a regular constitutional succession In that event his administration would have been considered but a mere eon stitutional continuance of the government of General Herrera, and the refusal of the latter to receive our minister would have been deemed conclusive, unless an intimation had been given by General I'aredes of bis desire

to reverse the decision of his predecessor. Hut the government of General Paredes owes its existence to a military revolution by which the subsisting constitutional authorities had been subverted. The form of government was entirely changed, as well as all the high functionaries by whom it was administered-

T -- 1 ' ' lm - - " Under these circumstances, Mr. Slidell, in obedience to mj direction, addressed a note to the Mexican minister of foreign relations, under date of the 1st of March last, asking to be received by that government in the diplomatic chancier to which he had been appointed. This minister, in bis reply under date of the 12th of March, reiterated the arguments of his predecessor, and, in terms that may be considered as giving just grounds of offence to the government and people of the United States, denied the application iff Mr Slidell. Nothing, therefore, remained for our envoy but to demand bis passports, and retain to his own country. Thus the government of Mexico, though solemnly pledged by official acts in Oetober last to receive and accredit an American envoy, violated their plighted faith, and refused the offer of a peaceful adjustment of our difficulties. Not only was the offer rejected, but the indignity of its rejection was enhanced by the manifest breach of faith in refusing to admit the envoy, who came bee ruse they had hound themselves to receive birn Nor can it be said that the offer w as fruitless from the want of opportunity of discussing it þÿ our envoy was" present on their own soil. Nor can it tie ascribed to a want of sufficient powers þÿ our envoy had full powers to adjust every question of difference. Nor was there room for complaint that our propositions for settlement were unreasonable þÿ permission was not even given our envoy to make any proposition whatever. Nor

can it be objected that we, on our part, would not listen to any reasonable terms of their þÿsuggestion the Mexican government refused all negotiation, and have made r.o proposition of any kind. In my message at the commencement of the present session, I informed you that, upon the earnest appeal both of the congress and convention of Texas, I had otdered an eflic.ient military force to take a position " between the Nueces and the Del None " This had become necessary, to meet a threatened invasion of Texas by the Mexican forces, for which extensive military preparations had been made. The invasion was threatened solely because Texas bad determined, in accordance with a solemn resolution of the Congress of the United States, to annex herself to our Unioi ! and, under these circumstances, it was plainly our duty to extend our protection over her citizens arid soil. This force was concentrated at Corpus Cliristi, and remained there tmlil after I bad received such information Iroin Mexico as rendered it probable, if not certain, thai the Mexican government would refuse to receive our envoy. | To be Concluded in our nexl.\

Tub SteaM-boa a Spanish Invention. þÿ To the curious in such matters the following statement, which we copy from a daily contemporary, will prove interesting; þÿ Although the honour of the invention of steamers is claimed by other nations, it belongs, in reality, to Spain alone, as can be pioved by histoiical facts as far back us the middle of the sixteenth century, during the reign of Chat Its the Fifth. The erudite and inlelli gent Don Martin Feinandiz de Navarette s ins in one of his works, that Don Biasco de G-irey, captain in the Spanish navv, submitted to the examination of the Emperor, in 1513, a machine, hv means of which vessels, no matter how large, could be navigated when not a breath of wind was stirring, and without the aid of sails or sweeps. Soon afterwards the Emperor ordered a trial to be made of it, which took place on the 1 7th of June, 1513, in Barcelona road, with the most complete success The cxpciimcitl was made upon a ship of 20t) ions called the

Santissima Trinidad, commanded by Captain Pedro de Soarsa, who had arrived at Barcelona. with a cargo of wheat- The persons present at the essay, by order of Churles V., and his son Philip IP, were Don Earique de Toledo, the Governor, Pedro de Cardona ; the Grand Treasurer liavigo; the Vice Chancellor Francisca Gralla, and a number of distinguished individuals from Castile and Catalonia, besides several naval officers, some of whom were on board the Santissima Trinidad, and others on stiore. This experiment which astonished all who beheld it by the facility and rapidity of the vessel's movements, caused a general vote in favour of the invention of Don Biasco de Garay, with the exception of the treasurer, Kuvago, who objected to it, principally on account ol the great cost of the machines, and the danger of the boiler bu: sting. T hus the stupid opposition o! liavago retarded, r.eaily 200 yeais, the realisation of the invention ol steam boats. Nevertheless, the Emperor promo'ed Garay, at the same time presenting him with 200,000 maravides, and defraying all the expenses lie had been at in bunging bis invention to fiui lion. Despite the uouble Garay took to bide the mechanism ol his invention, we see it consisted ol a holier tilled with water, agitated by heat for the generation of steam, and tw o moveable wheels attached to the sides of vessels. We are glad to learn that the great Southeritiine is to be commenced immediately. The vast importance and benefit of the telegraph, is but just beginning to be felt. It is beginning to be used as a medium, not only of business communication, but also in the various social relations of life. The mode of communication is so novel, socomplete, and so instantaneous, that people employ it for sending messages to their friends in another city, about every day household affairs. But in a commercial point of view, the advantages ate incalculable. These will be fully appiecialed without enumerating them. The rapidity with which news is now conveyed from the seat ol government to this city, is another striking illustration of the utility of the telegraph. During the late active operations of our army on the banks of the Rio Grande, the anxiety of our citizens for intelligence from the scat of war, was raised to the highest pitch; aud although it was satisfied by rapid interchange of intelligence between Washington and this oitv, owing to Ihe enterprising efforts of the cash papers to keep the public advised, at the earliest possible moment, of whatever transpired at Washington, _in relation to our gallant army, yet, if the commuicalion from New Orleans to this city had been unbroken

and complete, how much more satisfactory would it have been to receive the news as soon as it reached the metropolis of the South. But the actual saving of our government from the existence of such a line to our South western border has been strikingly illustrated by the fact that all the expense incurred by the calling out of the volunteers mustered by General Gaines might have beetr saved, had the government had hourly communication with that officer. The space of a fortnight þÿ the time occupied in mutual communication by letter between Washington and New Orleans, would have been auuihilated, had

there been a telegraphic communication between the two cities, and the government would have saved a million of dollars, ac cording to their own þÿaccount a sum more than sufficient to construct a telegraph over twice the distance between New Orleans and Washington. This fact speaks volumes in favor of the construction of a Southern line ot telegraph ; and we hope to see before many months, (it can easily be effected before the next session of Congress) an uninterrupted communication between our North eastern and Southwestern borders. This is by no means an Utopian prospect, and with such a communication we cannot but promise ourselves incalculable advantages. We will but instance one, out of the many benefits, likely to accrue from it þÿ namely, the case with which the villany of fotgers, burglars, defaulters, and other scoundrels of that description, could be foiled and counteracted. A robbery or forgery is committed in New York, and instantaneous intelligence is conveyed to Philadelphia, Uuliimot e, Boston, Albany, and all the principal cities in the Union. The officers of the law are immediately apprised of the rascality, and the rogue, upon stepping out of the cars or boat, as the case may tic, is arrested, and his evil designs are frustrated His villany travels before him on the wings of the lightning, and the consequences stare him in the face when he thinks himself most secure. As a proof that the enterprize of our citizens under out glorious institutions, is culled

into exercise more than in countries where republicanism does not exist, we may mention the fact that in England there ate but a little more than one hundred miles of telegraph as yet constructed, and in Prance a little more, notwithstanding the vast wealth of these countries, and the power of the govelements. To day the mortal remains of the deceased, alter having been embalmed, were exposed in theSixtine Chap- I and to morrow thev are to be transported in solemn pomp to the mid. tie of the principal nave of the Vatieian Church. To Destroy Moths. þÿ Spirit of turpentine is the best remedy against the grub of the common woollen moth, as wi II as aga rist that of all other insects. If a shallow vessel containing turpentine be placed in a waidrobe or drawers containing clothes, or wollen articles, furs, þÿ&e i , t immediately destroys any of the larvae of that insect, and so effectually, that hy properly moving and exposing the surface to its action when in a siaie of evaporation (which it will always attain, especially in warm weather), it will cause them to die, and appear on the surrounding shelves of the places in which clothes are deposited. The Ranciieros of Mexico þÿ The Kancheros, part of the material of the Mexican army, are half Indian and half Spanish in their extraction ; gaunt, shrivelled, though muscular m their ft air es, and datk and swarthy visnged as they are, these men ate the Arabs of the American continent. Living half of the time in the saddle, for thev are unr i vailed horsemen, with lasso in hand they traverse the vast plains in search of the Buffalo and wild horse. The killing of these animals and the preparation and sale of their hides are 1 heir sole means of livelihood þÿ Their costume generally consists of a pair of tough lode leggings, wuli sandals of the same material, bound together with leathern thongs, over which is a blanket wiih a hole in the centre large enough to allow the head to he thrust out, and which falls not ungracefully over their shoulders, leaving ample room for t ie play of their arms Add to this a broad straw sombrero, and the lasso hanging ready for use in his girdle, and you have the Ranchero as he appears in the time of peace. þÿ Join to this a long lance with a sharp spear head, and his belt plentifully supplied with pistols and knives, and you have Raw-hero us a member of a troop of banditti, or as a soldier in a body of cavalry. Their power

The ' following account of the last hours Pope Gregory of I, are taken from a letter received from Home : " On Whit Sunday, the Pont ill' determined to have mass said in his chamber, and to take the communion himself. This was opposed, and he was obliged to almost get angry in order to have his wish complied with ; and, if he had not done so, he would have died without the sacrament. His valet de cliambre said to bun, But, Holy Father, you will alarm the whole city ; they will say that you are very ill ' Certainly,' replied he, 'lam ' very ill; I feel it; and do you want me to appear before God without having taken the bread of life? to voglio rnorire da fratenon da sovro.no' (I wish to die as a monk, and not as a sovereign) The malady made such rapid progress the following night that the cardinal confessor, whose duty it is to assist dying Pontills, could not be summoned in time ; it was the assistant cure of the Pontifical Palace who gave extieme unction to the P ipe, the cme not having arrived. Gregory XVI had expired when Cardinal Bianehi. his confessor, entered his chamber. I he other ecclesiastics, who were summoned according to custom, had only to watch over the mortal remains of their master. The Pone nxpi-cd in the arms of Cardinal Lambruschini, who had hurried up with all ihe s ie d of his horses, and who assisted him in h s ins' moments with the tenderness of a friend and a son.'' Mathematical Physiognomy þÿ The form of the circle whose essence is the equi distance of every point of its circumference from iis centre with ihe most exact position does not convey an idea of beauty, wiulsl the þÿ freedom in the line of the oval has, by the elegance of its form, entitled it to be adopted foi the head of the last and master production of nature þÿ man. LIEBIG WHEN A BOY. Liebig was distinguished at school as a " booby," the only talent then cultivated in German schools being verbal memory, on one occasion, being sneeringly asked by the master what he proposed to become, since he was so bad a scholar, and answering that he would be a chemist, the whole school house burst into a laugh of derision. Not long ago Liebig saw his old school master who feelingly lamented his own former blindness. The only boy in ihe same school who ever disputed with Liebig the station of " booby," was one who could never learn his lesson by heart, but was continually corn posing music, and writing down by stealth in school. The san e individual Liebig lately found ai Vienna, distinguished as a composer and conductor of the Imperial Opera House. 1 think his name (s (Fuelling, li is to be hoped that a more rational system of school instruction is gaining ground. Can anything be more absurd or detestable than a system which made Walter Scott and Justus Liebig " boobies" at school, and so effectually concealed their natural talents, that, for example, Liehig was often lectured before the whole school on his being sure to cause misery and broken hearts to his parents, while he was all the time conscious, as the above anecdote proves, ol the possession of talents similar in kind to those he has since displayed. þÿ Phrenological Juui rial,
